label: Capacity at the end of the rated cycles
description: A car's rated cycles count full cycles until the battery has this much capacity left (% of nominal), unless the car states its own value. Sets the size of the cycle fade in the battery ageing and the years until this much capacity is left
source: Usual threshold of cycle ratings and battery warranties (70–80 %); the spreadsheet used 80 % as long-term capacity (Car Details row 7)

label: Capacity left shown green from
description: Battery life: capacity left after the years at or above this value is shown green. Colour only; there is no pass or fail, users judge for themselves
source: Judgement: user's choice 2026-11-21 (usual threshold of cycle ratings and battery warranties)

label: Capacity left shown red below
description: Battery life: capacity left below this value is shown red; between this and the green value orange
source: Judgement: user's choice 2026-11-21

label: Extra cycle wear from fast charging
description: Each full cycle charged at a DC fast charger counts as 1 + this × the charging rate (C = battery capacities per hour) cycles of wear, relative to typical habits. Lithium plating and heat at high charging rates
source: Fitted to INL's DC fast-charge study (four 2012 Nissan Leafs, 50,000 miles, charged twice a day): DC-only 50 kW packs lost 27.4 % vs. 24.8 % for AC Level 2 (INL/MIS-13-29877, 2014). Geotab 2026 shows a larger gap (1.5 vs. up to 3.0 %/year), but its fast-charging-heavy cars also drive more; the model reproduces it when they drive about twice as far (degradation_measurements.csv)

label: Typical fast-charging rate
description: Charging rate of the typical fleet car the ageing is fitted to (10 → 80 % in about 40 min). A car's own rate comes from its charging test (charge_from_pct → charge_to_pct in charge_time_min)
source: Assumption; the fleet data (Tesla, Geotab 2019–2024 models) charge at roughly 0.8–1.5 C

label: Charge while parked full
description: State of charge assumed for the time a car is parked above 80 % (calendar ageing rate from calendar_soc.csv)
source: Assumption: middle of 80–100 %

label: Charge while parked otherwise
description: State of charge assumed for the rest of the parked time
source: Assumption: middle of a typical 20–90 % daily range

label: Typical: share of charging at DC fast chargers
description: Typical habits = the fleet average the ageing is fitted to; the factors are 1 here
source: Geotab 2026: DC fast charging has grown to about 25 % of all charging sessions

label: Typical: time parked above 80 % charge
description: Typical habits = the fleet average the ageing is fitted to
source: Geotab 2026: most vehicles spend less than 80 % of their time at very high or low charge; 50 % = the border of its two lower groups

label: Gentle: share of charging at DC fast chargers
description: Preset "Gentle": mostly charged at home / AC
source: Geotab 2026 low group: under 12 % of sessions on DC

label: Gentle: time parked above 80 % charge
description: Preset "Gentle": charged to 80 % for daily use, to 100 % only before trips
source: Geotab 2026 low group: under 50 % of the time at extreme charge

label: Hard: share of charging at DC fast chargers
description: Preset "Hard": mostly fast-charged (no home charger)
source: Geotab 2026 high group: over 12 % of sessions on DC, many above 100 kW

label: Hard: time parked above 80 % charge
description: Preset "Hard": always charged to 100 % and left parked full
source: Geotab 2026 high group: over 80 % of the time at extreme charge

label: Battery heated below
description: While driving, thermal management heats the pack when it is colder than this
source: Facts tab (battery heating 0 kW from 10 °C); below that the cells' resistance rises steeply (see the battery tables)

label: Battery cooled above
description: Thermal management cools the pack when it gets warmer than this
source: Reviews quote an optimum of about 15–35 °C to 20–40 °C for Li-ion cells (e.g. Batteries 2024, 10(12):421). The Facts tab's 21 °C would mean cooling almost all year in Thailand

label: Max. battery heating/cooling power
description: Most heat put into or taken out of the pack
source: Facts tab: 2 kW

label: Battery heat loss to the air
description: Heat flow between pack and outside air per °C of difference. Packs are insulated and heavy (≈ 6–8 kJ/K per kWh), so they follow the air temperature only over many hours
source: Estimate: a parked Nissan Leaf pack (294 kg) cools with a time constant of about 9 h (owner measurement, mynissanleaf.com forum) ≈ 9 W/K; 15 W/K for larger packs and air flow while driving. Replaces the Facts-tab slope (200 W/K)

label: Nominal pack voltage
description: Only scales current; energy results do not depend on it
source: Typical 350–400 V passenger EV packs

label: Default cabin temperature
description: Starting value of the stress tests' cabin temperature (each test sets its own, or heating / AC off)
source: Argonne's tests hold 72 °F (22.2 °C)

label: People in the car
description: Body heat helps heating and adds to the AC load
source: Assumption: the driver

label: Body heat per person
description: Dry heat given off by a seated, moderately active person
source: ASHRAE Handbook – Fundamentals, Table 1 (people): moderately active office work 250 Btu/h sensible + 200 Btu/h latent = 73 W + 59 W (as tabulated in the Autodesk Revit help)

label: Body moisture per person (as heat)
description: Moisture the AC has to condense
source: ASHRAE Handbook – Fundamentals, Table 1 (people), see body heat

label: Cabin warming of a parked car in full sun
description: Temperature rise above the air of a car parked in 1000 W/m² of sun (scaled with the sunshine). Sets the cabin temperature at the start of a trip
source: McLaren, Null & Quinn 2005 (Pediatrics 116:e109): +40 °F (22 K) within an hour on clear days, whatever the air temperature

label: AC evaporator temperature
description: Cold side of the AC. It also dries the air: moisture condenses down to this dew point
source: Typical automotive evaporators run at 0–5 °C (frost limit)

label: AC condenser above air temperature
description: Hot side of the AC = air temperature + this
source: Typical 10–20 K

label: AC efficiency vs. the ideal (Carnot) cycle
description: COP = this × T_evap ÷ (T_cond − T_evap): 3.2 at 25 °C, 2.5 at 35 °C, 2.0 at 45 °C. Also used for battery cooling
source: Vapour-compression systems reach 30–50 % of the Carnot COP; checked against Argonne's 35 °C measurements (data/onboard/measurements.csv)

label: Heat pump condenser temperature
description: Hot side of the heat pump (warm supply air)
source: Assumption: supply air ≈ 40 °C

label: Heat pump evaporator below air temperature
description: Cold side of the heat pump = air temperature − this
source: Typical 5–10 K

label: Heat pump efficiency vs. the ideal (Carnot) cycle
description: COP = this × T_cond ÷ (T_cond − T_evap): 2.0 at 0 °C, 1.7 at −10 °C
source: Tesla Model 3 heat pump on a dynamometer (TEEL): COP 1.53–3.33 at 0 °C and 0.80–1.93 at −10 °C (Humphries & Loiselle-Lapointe 2026, reported by Zhang & He 2026, arXiv 2605.05919)

label: Heat pump covers all heating down to
description: Below this, a growing share comes from the resistive heater
source: Argonne BEV 1: 79 % of the heating power from the heat pump at −6.7 °C, 19 % at −17.8 °C (DOE Program Record, Sep 2024)

label: Heat pump off below
description: Below this only the resistive heater works
source: As above

label: Charging speed outside the fast-charge window
description: Share of the fast charging speed below/above the fast window
source: Car Details comment: assumed to half the fast charging speed

label: Charging efficiency (grid → battery)
description: Test-cycle consumption is measured from the grid; this converts it to battery energy, and battery energy back to paid energy
source: Assumption; typical AC charging 85–95 %

label: Tyre rolling resistance
description: Used when a car has no tyre_rr value; 8 N/kN = EU tyre label class C, measured at 80 km/h (ISO 28580)
source: EU tyre label (Regulation (EU) 2020/740) class C: 7.8–9.0 N/kN

label: Typical recommended tyre pressure
description: Tyre pressure is set as % of each car's recommended pressure (Conditions); this only sets how strongly rolling resistance reacts: ≈1.5 % per psi below it, +14 % at 80 % pressure
source: National Academies SR 286 (2006): ≈1.4 % per psi at 24–36 psi, 24 → 29 psi = −10 %; UN R141: tyre-pressure warning at 20 % loss; real cars: about 10 % low on average (US DOE), 12 % have a tyre ≥ 25 % low (NHTSA 2012)

label: Regenerative braking efficiency (wheel → battery)
description: Share of braking energy (and of downhill energy beyond air drag and rolling) that is recovered into the battery; it is spent again through the drivetrain, so a round trip returns about 70 % × the drivetrain efficiency
source: Assumption within the measured range: Boretti (SAE 2013-01-2872) finds a round trip near 70 % with a driving efficiency near 90 % (≈ 78 % wheel → battery); kept at 70 % (conservative) because the calibration of every car rests on it

label: Deceleration covered by regeneration alone
description: Braking up to this deceleration (0.2 g) is done by the electric motor; harder braking adds the friction brakes, whose share of the braking energy is lost as heat. The regenerative brake force is the car's effective mass × this deceleration
source: Series regenerative braking strategy: regeneration alone below 0.2 g, friction brakes blended in above (NPTEL, Brake System of EVs and HEVs, after Ehsani et al.); published blending limits range 0.1–0.3 g

label: Lowest speed with regeneration
description: Below this speed the friction brakes finish the stop (the motor's back-EMF is too small to brake effectively)
source: Kia owner's manual: regeneration control works above 10 km/h; Mazda: regeneration works best above about 15 km/h, friction brakes for the last few km/h. Typical hand-over 5–12 km/h

label: Typical slope of the hills
description: Slope of the climbs and descents when a test does not set one (Terrain inputs). The total climb is driven at this slope, the descent too; the rest of the trip is flat. Gentle descents are used almost completely against air drag and rolling, steeper ones go through regeneration
source: Between the steepest grades of main roads in rolling and mountainous terrain (AASHTO via WSDOT Design Manual 1220: 4–5 % rolling, 5–6 % mountainous)

label: Driving style: window of the local mean speed
description: The driving style scales each speed's deviation from the mean speed over this window (centred, stops included). 30 s is about one city stop-start; it makes the accelerations and braking scale nearly in proportion to the style
source: Model choice; the presets below are checked against the EU RDE dynamics bounds on the WLTP traces (tests/drivingStyle.test.ts)

label: Driving style preset: Gentle
description: Accelerations and braking at 65 % of the WLTP's: softer launches, slowing early instead of braking late
source: The smoothest driving the EU RDE test still accepts: relative positive acceleration (RPA) of the WLTP low phase at its lower bound −0.0016·v̄ + 0.1755 m/s² (Regulation (EU) 2017/1151, Annex IIIA, Appendix 7a)

label: Driving style preset: Sporty
description: Accelerations and braking at 170 % of the WLTP's: hard launches, higher peaks, late hard braking
source: The most dynamic driving the EU RDE test still accepts: 95th percentile of v·a⁺ of the WLTP city phases at its upper bound 0.136·v̄ + 14.44 m²/s³ (Regulation (EU) 2017/1151, Annex IIIA, Appendix 7a). Bingham et al. (2012) measured about 30 % more energy for aggressive than for moderate driving of an EV

label: Rotating mass factor
description: Extra effective mass of wheels and motor during acceleration
source: Typical 1.03–1.08 for single-speed EVs

label: Frontal area ÷ (width × height)
description: Used when a car has width and height but no frontal area
source: Common approximation for passenger cars

label: Default drivetrain efficiency
description: Only used if a car cannot be calibrated (no consumption and no range)
source: Assumption

label: Fuel of a warm engine at idle, per litre of engine size
description: Fuel a petrol engine burns just to keep turning (friction, pumping) with no load, × the car's engine_cc. It is burned all the time the engine runs: also standing in a jam (the engine stays on in traffic) and at the stops of the test cycle (no start-stop modelled). Driving, AC and electrics come on top at the engine's calibrated marginal efficiency
source: Argonne National Laboratory (Gaines, Rask, Keller 2013): 2011 Ford Fusion 2.5 l, warm engine, 21 °C, no accessories, direct fuel-flow meter: 0.279 cc/s = 1.0 l/h = 0.40 l/h per litre; passenger cars 0.2–0.5 gal/h (0.8–1.9 l/h) across sizes. Small modern engines may idle somewhat lower

label: Alternator efficiency
description: Electric loads of a petrol car (electronics, blower) come from the alternator: engine power = electric power ÷ this. The AC compressor is driven by the belt directly
source: Remy (Bradfield 2008): typical alternator 55 % (belt 98 %); 55 % to almost 80 % at full output for current production alternators

label: Energy in a litre of petrol (lower heating value)
description: Turns the fuel burned into heat: the engine's waste heat for the cabin heater, and the efficiencies shown
source: US DOE Alternative Fuels Data Center, Fuel Properties Comparison: gasoline/E10 112,114–116,090 Btu/gal (GREET 2019) = 31.2–32.4 MJ/l = 8.7–9.0 kWh/l

label: Share of the fuel energy that heats the coolant
description: Waste heat the cabin heater can use = this × the fuel burned per hour (idle, driving, AC and electrics). Heating beyond that needs extra fuel (the engine idles faster or works harder), of which again this share reaches the heater. A cold engine's warm-up is not modelled
source: Judgement: in the energy balance of petrol engines roughly a quarter to a third of the fuel energy goes to the coolant, more at light load and idle

label: Payload during the official test
description: Driver and test equipment on top of the curb weight
source: Assumption (WLTP test mass ≈ curb + 100 kg)

label: Test temperature
description: Ambient temperature of the official tests
source: WLTP and CLTC: 23 °C; NEDC: 20–30 °C

label: Standard assumed when a car has no rated range
description: Used to calibrate cars without any rated range
source: Assumption

label: Currency for comparisons
description: Currency for All markets; a market uses its own currency (data/markets.csv)

label: Running costs for All markets
description: Market whose running costs (data/running_costs.csv, data/road_tax.csv) apply under All markets and in markets without rows of their own, converted to the display currency

label: Exchange rate EUR → THB
description: Used to convert car prices and costs
source: Your Currency_Converter.ods (Frankfurter reference rates of 2026-09-18)

source: Your Currency_Converter.ods (Frankfurter reference rates of 2026-09-18)
